title: Almost 1,000 Interviews, Here’s What I Still Love About Hiring

There is also a responsibility that comes with all this curiosity Neda Golshan CPO @ZOOD (OrientSwiss), Co-founder @Livuvo.com, Ex-Chief Product Officer @Digikala.com, Leadership Hiring Recruiting Product Management Almost 1,000 Interviews, Here’s What I Still Love About Hiring Neda Golshan 12 min read · Oct 21, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size Beyond finding the right people, hiring has given me something I never expected: a window into how companies think, how products are built, and how people experience the organizations they work for. Over the past 15+ years, I have been working in product management, building products, leading teams, and helping organizations grow. Throughout these years, one responsibility has remained a surprisingly consistent part of my job: hiring people. I would estimate that, on average, 20–30% of my time has been spent on hiring-related activities. Reviewing candidates, conducting interviews, discussing assessments, making difficult decisions, and trying to convince talented people to join the teams I was building. Looking back, I think I have conducted close to 1,000 interviews with people from different countries, cultures, industries, and professional backgrounds. And after all these conversations, there is something I have realized about myself: I genuinely enjoy interviewing people. :) Not necessarily every part of hiring. Let’s be clear about that. Hiring can be exhausting. It is time-consuming, sometimes frustrating, and full of uncertainty. You can spend weeks interviewing talented people and still not find the right match. You can finally find someone you are excited about, only to lose them to another opportunity. Sometimes, you make what seems like the perfect decision, and months later, you realize you were wrong. Even today, with all the AI tools helping us screen resumes, organize candidate information, automate processes, and prepare assessments, the final decision still requires human judgment. And human judgment is not perfect. But this article isn’t about how to hire better, the ideal interview process, or the questions every hiring manager should ask. It’s about something else. It’s about the part of hiring I have come to love so much that, occasionally, I seriously think about switching careers and becoming a tech recruiter. :) And surprisingly, it has very little to do with recruitment itself. Every interview is a window into another company One of the things I have always loved about working in product is learning how other companies operate. We read case studies, follow industry leaders, attend conferences, listen to podcasts, and analyze products. We try to understand why certain companies succeed, why others struggle, and how different teams approach similar challenges. But there is a limitation to most of these sources. We usually see the version of the story that a company decides to share publicly. A successful product launch becomes a story about great execution. A strategic pivot becomes an example of visionary leadership. A growing organization presents its culture as one of its greatest competitive advantages. But what actually happened inside? What did the team think about that strategy? How was the decision made? Who challenged it? What went wrong during execution? How did people feel about the changes? This is where interviews become fascinating to me. When I sit with a candidate who has spent several years working at another company, I am not just speaking with a potential future colleague. I am speaking with someone who has experienced another organization from the inside. Someone who has attended its meetings, participated in its decisions, navigated its politics, celebrated its successes, and experienced its failures. Of course, one person’s experience is never the complete truth about an organization. But it is a perspective you rarely find in a corporate presentation or a public case study. And across hundreds of conversations, these perspectives become an incredible source of learning. You learn how decisions are really made As a product leader, decision-making has always been one of my biggest areas of interest. Every company claims to be data-driven, customer-centric, agile, innovative, or some combination of these. But what happens when the data contradicts the CEO’s opinion? What happens when the product team believes a feature should not be built, but the commercial team has already promised it to an important customer? What happens when the company needs to choose between short-term revenue and long-term product health? How are difficult prioritization decisions made? Who has the final say? And what happens when those decisions turn out to be wrong? These are the situations that reveal how organizations actually work. And candidates often provide interesting perspectives through the stories they share about their previous projects. I particularly enjoy asking people to walk me through decisions they participated in. Not simply what they delivered, but why they chose that direction, what alternatives were considered, and what happened afterward.
